questions.questionText: Why can a model reproduce bias even without anyone intentionally building a biased system?
options: Bias only ever comes from intentional design choices
Training data reflects real-world patterns (including historical, representation, and measurement biases), which the model faithfully learns from
Models are incapable of learning bias
Bias only affects image models, never text or tabular data
questions.correctAnswer: Training data reflects real-world patterns (including historical, representation, and measurement biases), which the model faithfully learns from
questions.explanation: Historical, representation, and measurement biases can all be present in data reflecting real-world inequities, and a model trained on that data learns those patterns regardless of anyone's intent.

questions.questionText: Why is there no single agreed-upon definition of "fairness" for a model?
options: There actually is one universal definition everyone uses

Multiple mathematically valid fairness definitions (demographic parity, equalized odds, individual fairness) can be mutually incompatible, so choosing which matters most is an application-specific judgment call
Fairness cannot be measured mathematically at all
Fairness only applies to classification models
questions.correctAnswer: Multiple mathematically valid fairness definitions (demographic parity, equalized odds, individual fairness) can be mutually incompatible, so choosing which matters most is an application-specific judgment call
questions.explanation: It's mathematically proven that these definitions generally can't all be satisfied simultaneously except in special cases, making the choice of which to prioritize a genuine, context-dependent decision.

questions.questionText: Why is evaluating a model's metrics per subgroup important, rather than just checking aggregate accuracy?
options: It isn't important, aggregate metrics always tell the full story
Strong overall accuracy can mask a large, hidden accuracy gap for a specific subgroup that aggregate numbers completely hide
Subgroup evaluation is only relevant for image classification
It's purely a legal requirement with no technical justification
questions.correctAnswer: Strong overall accuracy can mask a large, hidden accuracy gap for a specific subgroup that aggregate numbers completely hide
questions.explanation: A model can perform very well on average while performing much worse for a specific subgroup — a disparity invisible unless metrics are broken out per group rather than only evaluated in aggregate.
